_why: Google Play identifies this app by the certificate that signs the upload. Play prints the fingerprint it expects when it rejects a bundle; that value is recorded here so a build can be checked BEFORE it is uploaded rather than after. A certificate fingerprint is public - it is in every copy of the app - so this file holds no secret.

uploadCertificate.source: Play Console rejection message, closed testing upload, 2026-08-09
uploadCertificate.note: This is the UPLOAD key. Play App Signing re-signs with its own app signing key for distribution, so the fingerprint users see on a device is a different one.

knownWrongKeys.why: Generated beside an existing circuvent-upload.jks by tooling that only looked for its own filename. Signing with it produces a bundle Play refuses. Every local artifact built so far carries it: 1.10.0-12 (aab and apk), 1.11.0-13, 1.12.0-14 — so no local build has ever been the one Play accepted.
React Native's debug key. Its password is published, so a release signed with it is one anybody could forge.

searched: Downloads/circuvent-android/ — the same wrong .keystore, and three artifacts all signed with it
Desktop, Documents, Downloads, OneDrive, .android, .gradle, .expo — no other Android keystore
circuvent-upload.jks (24 July, PKCS12) — the only file older than every local build; will not open with the password on file, nor with the account password
whereIsTheRealKey.mostLikely: The first release was built by EAS (Expo's cloud build). EAS generates PKCS12 keystores and keeps them server-side with a generated password, which fits the .jks exactly: PKCS12 format, earliest date, no local password. eas.json is present in this repo and no Expo account is currently logged in on this machine.
recover: npx eas-cli credentials --platform android    # shows the keystore and its password; can download it
node scripts/try-keystore-password.mjs <password> <downloaded-keystore>   # confirms the fingerprint before any upload

If EAS does not have it either, Play Console > Setup > App signing > Request upload key reset. Play App Signing is enabled, so the app's real signing key is held by Google and is not at risk — only the upload key needs replacing.
